etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English mi, my, apocopated form of min, myn, from Old English mīn (“my, mine”), from Proto-West Germanic *mīn, from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz (“my, mine”, pron.) (possessive of *ek (“I”)), from Proto-Indo-European *méynos (“my; mine”).

Cognate with West Frisian myn (“my”), Afrikaans my (“my”), Dutch mijn (“my”), German mein (“my”), Swedish min (“my”). More at me.

quote.citation: 1671, John Milton, “The First Book”, in Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for John Starkey […], →OCLC, page 10, lines 165-166:
quote.text: From what conſummate vertue I have choſe / This perfect Man, by merit call'd my Son,

definitions.definition: First-person singular possessive determiner. See Appendix:Possessive#English.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: An abbreviation of an oath such as my word or my Lord

definitions.definition: Used to express surprise, shock or amazement.
